Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.

Original prompt, preserved verbatim before I touch it:

"Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop (or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection, undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS: Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses. Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout — if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won, best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3, card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone."

Now let me poke at this before anyone gets to feel good about it.

The prompt has two goals that are in direct tension and the prompt itself admits it: "do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game being playable and correct." That sentence is doing a lot of work and it's the one I'd hold every later phase to. Historically in this fleet, visual ambition wins and correctness quietly loses — half-built games, cards that don't actually validate moves, undo that only pops one frame instead of reversing state. I want it on record now: if a later phase has to cut scope, the cut comes out of the art system, never out of rules correctness. A gorgeous card back on a game where you can drop a red 7 on a red 8 is not a smaller success, it's the exact failure the prompt calls out by name.

Second thing I don't trust: "must win awards" and "Apple Design Award reel" are not testable. Nobody can verify that claim with a build. I want the contract to translate that into things that actually can be checked: (a) a custom, non-SF-Symbols glyph/typography system for all 4 suits and ranks that is visually consistent across all 52 cards, (b) a card back that's part of the same visual language, not a stock texture, (c) one identifiable signature interaction or material effect that shows up on the very first screen and in a static screenshot, (d) light and dark mode that use different art direction, not `.colorInvert()`. If those four are true, we say the visual bar was met. If the aspiration text stays as the only bar, no later phase can be held accountable for missing it, and no reviewer can be held accountable for waving it through.

Third: "all 52 cards" with a "consistent illustrated or generative pattern language" is a scope trap. Hand-illustrating 52 unique faces to a consistent standard is a huge amount of asset work for a small factory run — the realistic failure mode is 8 great cards and 44 reused generic templates, which fails the brief's own explicit test ("if a screen looks like a stock tutorial, it failed"). My read: the prompt is actually asking for a *systematic* design — a generative or parametric face system (shared type/icon set + programmatic layout rules) that produces all 52 correctly and consistently, not 52 independent illustrations. That should be locked in now as the intended interpretation, because if it's not stated as a decision, someone will either half-illustrate the deck or burn the whole build budget on card art and ship a thin game underneath.

Fourth, real risk area — "no third-party package" plus "spring-based drag" plus "believable flip/deal animation" means everything (shuffle RNG, drag physics, card z-ordering during multi-card tableau drags, flip animation, haptics) gets hand-built in SwiftUI/UIKit interop. That's exactly where past runs in this fleet have shipped broken or placeholder screens. I want a concrete regression checklist baked in now, because "looks correct in a screenshot" and "is correct" are different things for a card game: dragging a run of cards off the tableau must move the whole run, not just the top card; dropping on an invalid target must snap back, not silently vanish or duplicate; undo must actually restore prior game state including stock/waste position, not just the last visual move; win detection has to fire only on a genuine win (all 52 in foundations in order), never as a placeholder "you win" screen; new game must reshuffle with a real RNG, not the same seed every launch.

Fifth: the local-only constraint has some ambiguity I want resolved as a decision, not discovered later. "Zero network calls" — does that include disabling any implicit URLSession usage from system frameworks, and does it explicitly forbid CloudKit/iCloud sync of the saved game between devices? I'm assuming yes, fully forbidden, single-device local storage only (UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData with no CloudKit container) — this should be locked as a hard requirement so nobody "helpfully" adds iCloud sync later thinking it's harmless since it's still "local" data.

Sixth, stats/settings interactions that are underspecified and will cause visible bugs if not decided up front: does "best time" apply when the timer is off (my call: no timed run recorded, don't show a fabricated 0:00 or stale best time — show it as N/A rather than lying about a time that didn't happen, per the no-fake-state rule); are stats/best-time tracked separately per draw-1 vs draw-3 mode or combined (my call: track separately, since draw-1 and draw-3 have very different win rates and a combined "best time" or win streak is misleading); does switching draw mode or card back mid-game require finishing/abandoning the current game (my call: card back can change live, draw mode change prompts a new game since it changes legal deal state). These aren't fun details, they're exactly the kind of thing that becomes a "stats screen shows nonsense" bug report during verification.

Seventh: haptics can't be verified in a simulator screenshot or automated build check — that means "haptics on card moves/wins" is a requirement that verification will have to either check in code (correct API calls at the correct trigger points) or explicitly flag as unverified-by-simulator, not silently marked done.

For production-readiness, I don't want "compiles and runs" to count. My bar: a full game is playable start to finish with correct legal-move enforcement in both draw-1 and draw-3, undo works across multiple moves and restores exact game state, new-game deals a fresh correct shuffle every time, win is detected only on a true win, stats and settings persist across app relaunch (not just in-session state), light and dark mode both render the art-directed theme without any hardcoded literal colors/fonts outside the theme file, and there is no placeholder screen anywhere in the four core screens (game, stats, settings, plus whatever win/new-game affordance exists). Given this fleet's own logged history of blank-screen and hardcoded-color failures, I'd treat those two categories as automatic non-negotiable rejects for this app specifically.

Non-goals I'd write down explicitly so nobody scope-creeps or scope-cuts silently: no multiplayer, no other solitaire variants (Spider, FreeCell) even as a stretch, no in-app purchase or monetization of any kind, no iCloud/cross-device sync, no accounts, no analytics/crash reporting SDKs even "for quality," no landscape-specific redesign unless trivial (portrait-first is implied by "iOS" + solitaire convention, should be confirmed as the assumption), no achievements/game-center integration (that would touch network/sign-in, directly violating the central constraint even though it's an Apple system service).

Decision rule I want binding on every later phase: whenever visual ambition and rules-correctness compete for build time or complexity budget, correctness wins, and the reason must be logged, not silently resolved by shipping the prettier broken version.

Testable requirements pulled from the prompt, each independently checkable by playing the app:

1. The app makes zero network calls at runtime (verifiable via no networking APIs in code and no network activity when device is offline).
2. There is no sign-in, account creation, or any user-identifying flow anywhere in the app.
3. No analytics, telemetry, or crash-reporting SDK is present or fires any event.
4. All game state, stats, and settings persist on-device and survive app relaunch and airplane-mode use.
5. The game deals a real, correctly-shuffled Klondike layout (1 waste-visible stock pile, 4 foundations, 7 tableau columns with 1–7 cards, top card face-up).
6. Cards can be moved via drag (or tap-to-move) between tableau, foundation, and waste according to real Klondike legal-move rules (alternating color descending sequences on tableau, ascending same-suit on foundation).
7. Illegal moves are rejected/snapped back, never silently accepted or silently dropped.
8. Moving a run of stacked tableau cards moves the entire valid run together, not just the top card.
9. Undo reverses the last move and restores the full prior game state (including stock/waste position), and supports multiple consecutive undos.
10. New Game / redeal produces a freshly shuffled, playable layout every time (not a repeated/fixed deal).
11. Win is detected only when all 52 cards are correctly on the foundations, and a win state is never shown otherwise.
12. Card faces use an original custom typography/iconography system for all 52 cards and the back, not SF Symbols and not generic flat rounded-rect templates, and this system is visually consistent across the full deck.
13. Cards render with visible texture/shadow/lighting suggesting physical card stock, not flat vector fills.
14. Card motion (drag, deal, flip) uses spring/physics-based animation rather than linear/instant transitions.
15. Light mode and dark mode each have distinct, purpose-designed art direction (not one being a simple color-inversion of the other).
16. At least one identifiable signature visual/interaction "hook" is present and recognizable from a single static screenshot.
17. Haptic feedback fires on card moves and on winning the game.
18. A stats screen exists showing games played, games won, best time, and current streak, all computed from real local play history (no placeholder numbers).
19. A settings screen exists allowing draw-1 vs draw-3 selection, card back selection (at least 2 backs), and timer on/off, and each setting actually changes app behavior when toggled.
20. The app can be built and run as a real installable iOS app (not a prototype/spec) suitable for App Store submission review.
